This advanced system was specifically acquired to track the melt pool in-situ, providing unparalleled insights into the additive manufacturing process. With a projected installation date of September 16th, 2024, the team is eagerly anticipating the opportunities this technology will bring. Notably, the Peregrine system, at the time of procurement, was limited to processing powder bed-based images captured after recoating and lasing. In contrast, the PrintRite3D system will capture images in- line with the laser, offering a unique perspective on the laser's operation. The team plans to map these in-line laser images onto a global powder bed image once the PrintRite3D system is online, enabling a more comprehensive understanding of the melt pool dynamics and further enhancing the capabilities of the Peregrine system. Operational Delays Software The deployment of Peregrine was unfortunately delayed due to a series of unforeseen challenges. A critical issue arose with the EOS M290 software, which controlled two essential lights required for the sensors to capture high-quality images. Specifically, both the side light and top light needed to be activated simultaneously to achieve optimal picture quality. However, the software version at the time imposed a limitation, restricting operators to using only one light at a time, depending on the operation. During operation, the top light was not enabled, making it difficult to obtain clear images. To address this issue, an EOS technician was called in to update the software. Upon inspection, it was discovered that the computer embedded in the EOS M290 platform was also outdated, necessitating a comprehensive hardware and software update. Unfortunately, this process took several weeks to complete, largely due to the limited availability of EOS technicians, further delaying the deployment of Peregrine. Procurement The procurement process for the sensors proved to be a lengthy and arduous one, beset by unexpected delays and setbacks. Initially, team members submitted a request for the sensors, but the orders languished for months, failing to be processed in a timely manner. To make matters worse, one of the quotes expired due to neglect, further complicating the situation. Even after the orders were finally processed, the sensors were subjected to a rigorous vetting process by global security to assess the risk of their usage at the laboratory. This scrutiny was necessary because the sensors, by design, store some information on board, including frame buffers, which raised concerns about potential security risks.
